# From prompting to a factory

## terminology

- Settle the terms before teaching anything (01, 06):

Before we dive into the book, we need to define a few terms we'll use throughout. After you have some basic terminology, let's jump into some of the high-level patterns and practices you'll see throughout the book.  These will serve you well, no matter how much of the remainder of the book you read, and no matter what platforms or frameworks you choose to build your own agents in.

An **agent** is a container for one or more tasks: a way to make their execution reliable and repeatable. You can think of it as a highly simplified human being, trained to perform specific tasks over time. The agent is not the task itself, though. The task is carried out through a **workflow**: the sequence of steps that together accomplish one piece of work. If you’re coming from Anthropic’s approach, distinguish those steps from the sessions in which they run: a workflow describes the work, not how its execution is divided across sessions.

Agency: Your definition of “ability to act without relying on another person” explains what makes an agent more than a container.

A **model** is a representation of patterns or relationships that a system uses to turn inputs into outputs. Depending on the model, those outputs might be a prediction, a decision, a numerical representation, or newly generated content. A model is a tool an agent can use, not what makes it an agent. If fixed rules and heuristics are enough to carry out the task, the agent may not need a model at all.
First of all, there are several types of models; most often you'll see me refer to decision models, like Jev, or generative models like Llama.  Even within generative models, you can further categorize models as embedding models -- models that can categorize into non-discrete categories.  These are useful for turning a body of text into notes or for finding content patterns within it.  You can have image, video, or audio generators versus text generators.  You have generative models that specialize in reasoning and in text generation for a specific purpose, like code writing.  

Reliability: You already promise it in the agent definition; briefly establish what counts as success and how you’ll measure it.
When I speak about reliability, it's more than a simple metric. It's all the aspects of an entity that add up to your being able to rely on it doing what you expect.  Reliability isn't necessarily the same thing as deterministic as a computer scientist would use it.  Especially considering models themselves are statistics-based, and not deterministic.  But when we built automation and now build agentic workflows, we still need to be able to rely on what we've built to do what we designed it to do.

That means we build in controls to limit hallucinations. We limit the chance that our automations run into false-positive or false-negative cases.  We limit their chance of doing something wildly unexpected, like deleting all the email in your inbox, leaking secrets, or failing to open the pod-bay doors.


The **harness** is the structure that runs that workflow—the wrapper around its prompts, tools, and execution environment. It might take the form of an agent loop or an orchestrator. In these terms, the discrete sessions, fresh context, and continuity through git and progress files described in Anthropic’s approach are harness choices: ways to manage execution and carry state from one session to the next. A versioned, pinned template and an agent-environment-session state machine likewise describe how that machinery is organized, rather than changing what an agent or workflow means here. Put simply, the workflow describes what needs to happen; the harness provides the machinery that makes it happen.

Factory: Define the organizing metaphor in the chapter title—how agents, workflows, and harnesses fit into your existing DevOps and CI/CD practices.

## patterns and practices

- An agent doesn't need a model. The heuristics-only `pr-review` is an agent: "the model is just a tool". Agency is "the ability to go do something without relying on another person" (01).
- "Agent, agency, etc, they are just this technology's words for automation. the same thing I've built for decades now." (01)
- What the LLM adds: "the way to handle probabilities and variation", for "the parts of automation that aren't 100% if then, then that" (01).
- The factory is CI/CD at agent velocity: "it's the same reason we build CICD -- it's just now we are building smarter guardrails and patterns to handle greater velocity" (03).
- "Reliable", in the agent definition, is what the rest of the book measures (01).
- No "AgentOps". Use DevOps and CI/CD terms; if the word appears, it comes with a joke that it's a hype word (05, decision).
- How to read vendor sources: "when talking to a hammer sales person, they'll try to convince you everything is a nail" (01).
- You're not starting from zero: "we know how it was done in the past… so we can PRIORITIZE reaching MVP over covering every theoretical" (06).
- The book's purpose: "help others avoid mistakes I've made and build a better solution". The failures are the material (05).

## What I use it for (evidence)
- **Databricks development work** (name nothing more specific: publication rule): 200 PRs in 14 days from 8 contributors. Asked for 3 significant changes in a 3-hour session, ours was the only team to finish all three through deployment (`vault: ideas/book-evidence-2026-11` §1).
- The Forgejo trend: merged PRs per month went 118 (Jun) → 1,130 (Sep) → 1,030 (Oct). Give the reader the caveats with it (credential ≠ worker; merge-on-green; volume ≠ value) (§2).
